reasons.D: Closest movement: runs of short, flat declaratives ('It has no taps.' 'A child could do it.'), a playful whimsy near the passage's, and a stammering dash ('is—well,'); the formal 'I will own' and 'I shall say nothing more' still feel more essayist than the author.
reasons.B: Plain diction and short, repeated imperative-like sentences ('Turn it a little... Turn it a little more...') echo the passage's simplicity, but it is smoother, more modern and more first-person-reflective than the author's clipped, oddly inverted sentences.
reasons.C: Long, balanced periodic sentences with semicolons and a genteel 'I confess'/'to be sure' register; the humour is urbane rather than the passage's deadpan and fragmented.
reasons.A: The most Latinate and British-essayist ('civilisation', 'extremities', 'I cannot entirely dismiss from my mind'), with long subordinate-heavy sentences and parentheses, the furthest from the passage's terse, telegraphic movement.
